critique.title: Fragmented Continuity #7
critique.medium: Encaustic and rust on birch panel
critique.label: This work interrogates the phenomenology of domestic ephemera through a lens of post-structural ambivalence. The artist's gesture simultaneously affirms and negates the material presence of the quotidian object.
critique.critique:
To encounter Fragmented Continuity #7 is to confront the limits of perceptual coherence. Ingrid Sørensen has constructed what appears, at first glance, to be a straightforward study in Encaustic and rust on birch panel—but sustained attention reveals the work's essential paradox. The image, if we can call it that, operates in deliberate tension with its own conditions of possibility.

The artist works within a tradition that refuses tradition, creating what art historian Felix Rasmussen identifies as 'anti-monuments to the contemporary.' The piece was created using a hybrid methodology that combines digital manipulation with analog degradation—each process meant to undo the certainties established by the other.

What results is neither image nor object but what critic Sanne Vestergaard terms a 'document of its own impossibility.' The work has been exhibited widely in contexts that emphasize this categorical ambiguity—most notably in 'The Unfinished Archive,' a 2021 exhibition at WIELS Contemporary Art Centre that examined art's relationship to incompletion.

Fragmented Continuity #7 ultimately refuses the viewer's desire for resolution. It proposes instead a model of meaning as perpetually deferred, always arriving and never quite present. In this way, Ingrid Sørensen's practice aligns with what theorist Lars Bergman calls 'the aesthetics of the almost'—art that lives in approximation rather than arrival.
provenance: Private collection, Oslo (acquired directly from artist, 2019)
Estate of Marius Hendriksen, Copenhagen (gift from unknown donor, 2020)
Sold at auction, Christie's London (provenance disputed, 2021)
Current location unknown (last recorded in Berlin, 2023)

critique.title: Study in Temporal Displacement
critique.medium: Mixed media with industrial felt and resin
critique.label: The piece operates within a framework of radical banality, foregrounding the latent violence of categorization itself. What appears as documentation reveals itself as pure construction.
critique.critique:
Dimitri Kostas's Study in Temporal Displacement emerges from a body of work concerned with what the artist describes as 'the aesthetics of institutional failure.' The piece foregrounds materiality not as presence but as a kind of structural absence—the thing that remains when use-value has been extracted and discarded.

Executed in Mixed media with industrial felt and resin, the work demonstrates the artist's commitment to processes that resist mastery. During its creation, Dimitri Kostas employed a method borrowed from obsolete industrial protocols, deliberately introducing errors at every stage of production. The result is a surface that refuses stability, that seems to shift under sustained observation.

The piece gained significant attention following its inclusion in the 2019 survey 'Objects Without Qualities' at the Berlinische Galerie, where critic Petra Svensson noted its 'aggressive refusal of affect.' Indeed, Study in Temporal Displacement seems to operate in a register beyond emotional response, in what philosopher Anna Kristeva has termed 'the post-affective sublime.'

Yet this apparent coldness masks a deeper engagement with vulnerability. As Dimitri Kostas has stated, the work's detachment is itself a performance—a way of holding space for something that cannot be directly named or shown. The viewer is positioned not as witness but as participant in this failure to cohere.
provenance: Originally part of a series of twelve, this is reportedly number seven of nine
Acquired by The Institute for Indeterminate Studies, Vienna (2019)
De-accessioned and sold to fund acquisition of works by the same artist already in collection (2021)
Current owner prefers to remain anonymous but is known to the artist

critique.title: Document of Impossibility
critique.label: Through careful orchestration of chromatic dissonance, the work proposes an alternative temporality—one that refuses linear narrative in favor of recursive encounter.
critique.critique:
In Dimitri Kostas's practice, we encounter a rigorous excavation of the everyday's hidden architectures. Document of Impossibility exemplifies this commitment to what the artist terms 'strategic misapprehension'—a deliberate refusal of the object's intended utility in favor of its phenomenological residue.

The work's surface bears the traces of what curator Maris Hendriksen has called 'the impossible document.' Here, representation collapses into its own mise-en-abyme, each layer of meaning simultaneously asserting and undermining the next. The piece was executed using a technique the artist developed during a residency in an abandoned textile factory—a process involving repeated exposure to controlled moisture followed by aggressive desiccation.

What emerges is less object than threshold, less image than index of seeing itself. The work participates in what theorist Jakob Vestergaard identifies as 'post-evidentiary practice'—art that operates after the collapse of truth claims, in the space where certainty once resided. The viewer confronts not representation but the ghost of representation, haunted by its own impossibility.

Critically, Document of Impossibility refuses recuperation into either formalist or conceptual lineages. It exists, uncomfortably, in the gap between these modes—a gap that, as the artist insists, is the only honest space remaining to contemporary practice.
exhibitions: 'Documents of Doubt,' Room for Time, Berlin (2020)
